"Complimentary" (adjective) has two distinct meanings. Both are in everyday use, and knowing both is essential.

When someone says kind, flattering, or positive things about a person, place, object, or action, we say those words (or that person) are complimentary.

Think of it this way: a "compliment" is a nice thing you say to someone. So "complimentary" simply means in the nature of a compliment — saying something good.

Examples:

  • "The professor was very complimentary about her essay."

(The professor said good things about it — praised it.)

  • "He wrote a complimentary review of the restaurant."

(The review was full of praise.)

  • "She wasn't very complimentary about my haircut."

(She didn't say nice things about it — notice this use is slightly ironic or negative in tone, meaning she was critical.)

  • "They exchanged complimentary remarks at the ceremony."

(They said kind, appreciative things to each other.)

Key point: When used this way, complimentary describes either the words/remarks themselves, or the person saying them. You can say "complimentary words," "a complimentary tone," or "she was complimentary."

The opposite of this sense would be: critical, harsh, unflattering, disparaging.

This is probably the meaning you'll encounter even more often in daily life. When a product or service is given to you at no cost, as a gesture of goodwill or courtesy, it is called complimentary.

This is different from just saying something is "free." The word complimentary specifically implies it is being given to you graciously — as a gift or courtesy — often by a business, host, or organisation. It's a polite, formal way of saying "you don't have to pay for this."

Examples:

  • "The airline offered complimentary snacks on the flight."

(The snacks were free — passengers didn't pay extra for them.)

  • "Guests receive complimentary Wi-Fi at this hotel."

(Wi-Fi is included at no charge.)

  • "He received two complimentary tickets to the concert."

(The tickets were given to him for free.)

  • "The spa includes a complimentary welcome drink."

(A free drink is included as part of the experience.)

  • "Please help yourself to complimentary coffee in the lobby."

(The coffee is available at no cost.)

Key point: This sense of the word is very common in hospitality, travel, events, and business. Whenever a company wants to say "we're giving you this for free as a nice gesture," they reach for the word complimentary. It sounds more gracious and formal than just saying "free."
The connection between the two meanings

You might wonder: how are these two meanings related? They both come from the same root idea — a compliment. In the first sense, you're paying someone a verbal compliment. In the second sense, you're paying someone a material compliment — giving them something as a gesture of goodwill. Both are acts of generosity or kindness, just expressed differently. So when a hotel gives you a complimentary breakfast, they are, in a sense, "complimenting" you as a guest with a kind gesture.
The one mistake almost everyone makes: Complimentary vs. Complementary

This is extremely important. There are two different words that sound identical but are spelled differently and mean completely different things. Many people — even native English speakers — confuse them.

WordSpellingWhat it means
ComplimentaryC-O-M-P-L-I-M-E-N-T-A-R-YPraising someone, OR given free
ComplementaryC-O-M-P-L-E-M-E-N-T-A-R-YTwo things that go well together, complete each other, or enhance each other

Complimentary (with an i) = praising, or free of charge.

Complementary (with an e) = things that complete or enhance each other.

Examples of complementary (the other word, just so you never confuse them):

  • "Red wine and cheese are complementary flavours." (They go well together.)
  • "The two teammates had complementary skills." (One was strong where the other was weak — together they were complete.)
  • In medicine: "complementary therapy" means a treatment used alongside conventional medicine.

A simple memory trick: compliMent (with an i) → think of "I want to pay you a compliment" → leads to complimentary. ComplemEnt (with an e) → think of "complEte" → leads to complementary (things that complete each other).

"Complimentary" as an adjective does one of two jobs in a sentence:

Job 1: It tells you that someone or something is expressing praise. ("She was very complimentary." / "A complimentary remark.")

Job 2: It tells you that something is being provided without charge. ("Complimentary breakfast." / "A complimentary upgrade.")

Both uses are correct, standard English, and you will encounter both regularly in books, conversations, hotels, newspapers, and everyday life. The context will almost always make it clear which meaning is intended — if someone says "the critic was very complimentary," they clearly mean praise; if someone says "enjoy your complimentary drink," they clearly mean it's free.
